questions.q: How was the dominance of the Congress restored under Indira Gandhi by 1971?
answer: After the setback of 1967 and the split of 1969, the Congress under Indira Gandhi recovered its dominance dramatically by 1971.

answer.text: In 1969 the Congress split into the Congress (O), led by the older Syndicate leaders, and the Congress (R), led by Indira Gandhi. Freed from the control of the old guard, she projected herself as a bold, decisive leader close to the people.

Indira Gandhi adopted a strongly populist and pro-poor programme. She nationalised the major banks, abolished the privy purses of the former princes, and raised the powerful slogan of Garibi Hatao, or Remove Poverty. These steps won her the support of the poor, minorities and weaker sections.
In the 1971 general elections her Congress won a sweeping majority, and the victory in the war that created Bangladesh soon after further boosted her standing.

answer: Thus, through new leadership and populist appeal, Indira Gandhi restored Congress dominance around herself.

questions.q: How did Indian politics change with the end of Congress dominance after 1967?

answer.text: marked a turning point, as Congress dominance began to break down and Indian politics became more competitive.

list: The Congress lost power in several states to opposition coalitions for the first time
Its majority at the centre was greatly reduced
Non-Congress and coalition governments appeared in the states, and defections became common
Regional parties and new leaders rose, and though Indira Gandhi later restored Congress dominance, the era of unchallenged one-party rule was ending

questions.q: How did Indira Gandhi restore and reshape the dominance of the Congress by 1971?

answer.text: restored Congress dominance by 1971 by reshaping the party and appealing directly to the people.

list: After a split in the Congress in 1969, she led her own faction and freed herself from the old party bosses
She adopted bold pro-poor, socialist measures like the nationalisation of banks and the abolition of princely privileges
Her slogan 'Garibi Hatao' (remove poverty) appealed to the poor and disadvantaged
